name: funtrace
baseline: LLVM XRay and uftrace function tracers (not perf, gprof or Valgrind)
workload: Per-call/return overhead of compiler-instrumented function tracing in the repo's simple-example microbenchmark.
claimed_speedup: <10 ns per instrumented call or return; 6x faster than an XRay microbenchmark (flight recorder logging), 15-18x faster than XRay basic logging, 4.5x faster than a uftrace microbenchmark
compiler_and_flags: gcc -finstrument-functions / -pg -mfentry -minstrument-return=call; clang -finstrument-functions / -fxray-instrument (flags stated for the instrumented builds, not for the comparison harness)
tradeoffs: Tracing profiler (timeline of calls), not a sampling profiler; x86-64 Linux; must be told what to trace; trace buffer is a flight recorder so old events are overwritten; needs recompilation with instrumentation flags.
caveats: Author's own microbenchmark; comparison numbers are in the README only, hardware not stated; baseline is XRay/uftrace, not perf/gprof/Valgrind; the author notes uftrace has different design goals. The linked blog post was blocked, so only the README was read.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'tracing profiler faster than uftrace OR XRay -finstrument-functions per call overhead' surfaced yosefk.com blog post 'Profiling in production with function call traces' and the repo

name: heaptrack
workload: Heap allocation profiling of real applications; LD_PRELOAD interposition of malloc versus Valgrind binary translation.
claimed_speedup: Qualitative only in README: overhead in time and memory 'significantly lower' than massif, multi-threaded apps not serialized, CPU-bound code not slowed. Blog and secondary sources describe about 1 order of magnitude slowdown for heaptrack versus up to 2 orders for Massif (snippet only, not verified).
license: LGPL-2.1-or-later (repo carries several licenses in LICENSES/: Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, BSL-1.0, GPL-2.0-or-later, LGPL-2.1-only, LGPL-2.1-or-later, MIT; main license not confirmed)
tradeoffs: Only tracks heap allocations (no CPU profiling, no leak detection of non-heap memory); Linux only; interposes malloc via LD_PRELOAD so stripped or static allocators may be missed.
caveats: No numbers in the README; the milianw.de blog post (found via search) was not opened. Tier D kept because the project is notable and the Valgrind comparison is explicit.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'heap profiler faster than Valgrind massif heaptrack overhead blog' surfaced Milian Wolff's heaptrack blog post and README

name: bytehound
workload: Heap allocation profiling with stack traces using a custom stack unwinder via LD_PRELOAD.
claimed_speedup: README: custom stack unwinding makes it 'a lot cheaper than other similar tools', 'potentially up to orders of magnitude faster in some cases' than heaptrack; no numbers.
tradeoffs: Rust (works on C/C++ programs through LD_PRELOAD); builds need nightly Rust and Yarn; Linux only; no longer actively developed.
caveats: No benchmark numbers or methodology; claim is qualitative. Last commit July 2023.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'bytehound memory-profiler heap profiler faster than heaptrack valgrind' results describing its custom unwinder

name: magic-trace
workload: Intel Processor Trace based capture of every function call in a snapshot window (about 10 ms) around a chosen function, versus sampled stacks.
claimed_speedup: 2%-10% slowdown (most apps near 2%), traces every call at about 40 ns resolution; wiki says overhead is lower than perf -g but higher than perf -glbr.
hardware: Requires Intel CPU with Processor Trace; specific model not stated on the page
tradeoffs: Intel PT only (no AMD, limited in VMs), snapshots only the last few milliseconds, uses memory bandwidth (hundreds of Mbps), decode errors if bandwidth saturates; needs perf and kernel support. Tool is OCaml but profiles C/C++ native binaries.
caveats: First-party wiki, no benchmark code or CPU model; it is a different kind of tool (high-resolution trace) than perf sampling, so the 'faster' claim is only about overhead versus perf -g. Jane Street blog post was not opened.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Intel PT magic-trace low overhead tracing blog Jane Street'

name: Dr. Memory
workload: Memory error checking on SPEC CPU2006 using DynamoRIO instead of Valgrind.
claimed_speedup: CGO 2011 paper (via search snippet): average slowdown 10.2x versus native for Dr. Memory against 20.4x for Memcheck, about 2x faster on average and up to 4x on single benchmarks; Valgrind could not run 434.zeusmp and 447.dealII (README confirms the second point).
tradeoffs: Memory checker rather than profiler; Windows, Linux, macOS and Android; older Valgrind versions compared in the paper.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (CGO 2011) but the PDF was blocked here, so the 10.2x and 20.4x figures are from a search snippet and the README only confirms 'faster'. Valgrind has changed since 2011. License is stated by the page as LGPL; SPDX version not confirmed.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Dr. Memory faster than Valgrind Memcheck slowdown'

name: Tracy Profiler
baseline: No perf, gprof or Valgrind comparison; manual compares profiled versus unprofiled run only
workload: Image compression benchmark with 16777216 zones per image; overhead of recording zone start and end events.
claimed_speedup: 2.25 ns per zone (includes start and end events), from the manual's performance impact section (derived from 37.7 ms mean run time difference over 16777216 zones).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC on x86 (Ryzen 9 3900X) for the neighbouring compression table; exact flags for the overhead benchmark not confirmed
hardware: Ryzen 9 3900X (stated for the manual's client compression table; overhead benchmark hardware not confirmed)
tradeoffs: Instrumentation (zones) plus sampling; needs source macros for zones; network server/viewer architecture.
caveats: Weak fit: no named baseline from perf, gprof or Valgrind is measured; overhead number is against the unprofiled program. Third-party blogs quote about 15 ns per zone, which differs from the manual's 2.25 ns. Included for orchestrator judgement; may be dropped.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Tracy profiler nanosecond overhead instrumentation per zone cost'
